title: WHY DID BIBLICAL KINGS HAVE CONCUBINES—AND WHY COULD SLEEPING WITH A KING’S CONCUBINE BECOME A POLITICAL ACT?
paragraphs: WHY DID BIBLICAL KINGS HAVE CONCUBINES—AND WHY COULD SLEEPING WITH A KING’S CONCUBINE BECOME A POLITICAL ACT?

The disturbing royal custom hiding behind some of the Bible’s strangest stories—and the breathtaking difference between the kings who took women to prove their power and the King who gave Himself to save His Bride.
There is a scene in the Bible so disturbing that most people read it quickly, feel uncomfortable, and move on.
A prince walks onto a rooftop.
A tent is erected where the nation can see it.
Ten women who belonged to his father’s household are brought to him.
And then, publicly, deliberately, in an act designed to send a message across Israel, Absalom sleeps with his father David’s concubines.
It sounds like sexual depravity.
It was.
But it was also something more.
It was politics.
It was rebellion.
It was a declaration of war.
And once you understand what a royal concubine represented in the ancient world, several strange passages of Scripture suddenly begin connecting like pieces of a puzzle.
Why did Ish-bosheth become furious when Abner was accused of sleeping with Saul’s concubine Rizpah?
Why did Absalom publicly take David’s concubines?
Why did Solomon react so severely when his older brother Adonijah asked to marry Abishag?
And perhaps the uncomfortable question beneath all of them:
Why did biblical kings have concubines in the first place?
Before answering, we need to establish something Christians sometimes forget when reading the Old Testament:
The Bible faithfully recording an action does not mean God is approving that action.
Scripture is brutally honest.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not sanitize kings.
It does not pretend powerful men were righteous simply because God used them.
The Bible will show you David worshiping.
Then David lusting.
David trusting God.
Then David manipulating.
David writing psalms.
Then David destroying a family.
That honesty is one reason Scripture feels so painfully human.
God does not need to hide His servants’ scandals to protect His reputation.
He exposes human sin because ultimately the Bible is not the story of impressive men rescuing themselves.
It is the story of sinners desperately needing a Savior.
And concubinage belongs inside that broken world.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pîlegeš.

A concubine was not simply the ancient equivalent of a casual girlfriend or modern mistress. She occupied a recognized domestic and sexual relationship with a man, but generally without the full status, security, or privileges associated with a primary wife.
That distinction matters.
Because when kings accumulated wives and concubines, women could become entangled with dynasty, inheritance, alliances, prestige, household expansion, succession, and royal power.
But we must never confuse what kings practiced with what God originally designed.
Long before Israel had palaces...
before David...
before Solomon...
before royal harems...
Genesis takes us into a garden.
One man.
One woman.
A covenant union.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — vehayu levasar echad
“and they shall become one flesh.”
Jesus Himself later reaches back to this creation account when teaching about marriage.
That is enormously important.
When Jesus explains marriage, He does not point to Solomon’s household.
He points to Eden.
The kings are not the standard.
Creation is.
And Israel’s kings were specifically warned against multiplying wives.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of the king that he must not יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים — yarbeh-lo nashim, multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
God knew what human beings keep discovering the painful way:
What looks like an expansion of power can become an expansion of bondage.
What looks like possession can eventually possess you.

Solomon became perhaps the most spectacular example. The king famous for wisdom eventually became the king whose multiplied relationships helped turn his heart away from wholehearted faithfulness to God.
So when Scripture tells us that kings possessed many women, the correct conclusion is not, “God must have endorsed royal harems.”
Sometimes Scripture describes the disease before showing us the consequences.
And now the story gets darker.
Because in the royal world, a king’s women could become connected with the king’s throne.
That helps explain one explosive confrontation after Saul’s death.
Saul was gone.
His dynasty was collapsing.
David’s kingdom was rising.
Saul’s surviving son Ish-bosheth occupied a fragile throne while Abner, Saul’s powerful military commander, increasingly held enormous influence.
Then one accusation detonated between them.
Saul had possessed a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.
Ish-bosheth confronted Abner over allegedly sleeping with her.
To modern ears, the reaction can seem disproportionate.
Why would an accusation involving one woman threaten a kingdom?
Because this was not necessarily heard merely as:
“You slept with my father’s woman.”
It could carry the terrifying political implication:
“Are you reaching for my father’s throne?”
The biblical narrative immediately turns toward royal legitimacy and transfer of the kingdom. Abner becomes enraged, breaks with Ish-bosheth, and moves toward transferring allegiance to David.
One woman stands at the center of a political earthquake.
And painfully, Rizpah herself barely gets a voice.
That should bother us.
Because one of the Bible’s recurring exposures of fallen power is how easily powerful people turn human beings into instruments.
She had a name.
Rizpah.
Not merely “Saul’s concubine.”
Not merely a royal possession.
A woman.
A mother.
A human being bearing God’s image.
Later Scripture gives us an unforgettable picture of Rizpah grieving over her dead sons, guarding their bodies with staggering maternal devotion.
The woman whom political history could reduce to somebody’s concubine emerges as a grieving mother.
That is worth remembering.
Behind the scandals of kings were real women.
Real tears.
Real consequences.
Real human beings caught inside the ambitions of powerful men.
Then comes Absalom.
And here the political symbolism becomes unmistakable.
Absalom is David’s son.
Handsome.
Charismatic.
Ambitious.
Wounded.
Dangerous.
He slowly steals the hearts of Israel, undermines his father, gathers supporters, and launches a rebellion.
David flees Jerusalem.
But David leaves ten concubines behind to maintain the palace.
Then Ahithophel gives Absalom horrifying advice.
Sleep with your father’s concubines.
Why?
Because Israel will hear about it.
That detail changes everything.
This was meant to become public knowledge.
Absalom was not merely indulging private lust.
He was making an irreversible public declaration.
So a tent was erected on the palace roof.
And Absalom went in to his father’s concubines “in the sight of all Israel.”
Think about the symbolism.
The son has entered the father’s capital.
The son occupies the father’s palace.
The son claims access to women belonging to the father’s royal household.
The message could hardly be louder:
David’s reign is finished. I am taking his place.
Sex became propaganda.
A bedroom became a battlefield.
Bodies became political territory.
And the roof itself carries a haunting irony.
Because years earlier David had walked on a rooftop and seen Bathsheba.
David’s sexual sin had begun in secrecy.
Nathan the prophet later announced that consequences would erupt publicly.
Now another rooftop appears.
Another sexual scandal.
Except this time all Israel is meant to see.
Sin has a terrible way of promising privacy while producing consequences far beyond the room where it began.
That does not mean every tragedy in a family is a direct punishment for a particular parental sin.
Scripture does not permit such simplistic conclusions.
But David’s story does show something terrifyingly real:
Our sins rarely remain as private as we imagine.
One hidden decision can wound marriages.
Children.
Trust.
Friendships.
Churches.
Generations.
You may hide the browser history.
Hide the messages.
Hide the relationship.
Hide the addiction.
Hide the bitterness.
Hide the secret account.
Hide the compromise.
Hide what happened when nobody else was watching.
But there is Someone from whom darkness cannot hide you.
And strangely...
that is not only terrifying.
For the repentant sinner, it can become the beginning of freedom.
Because the God who sees what you hide is also the God before whom you no longer have to pretend.
Maybe that is why this story is hitting you harder than you expected.
Maybe your scandal never involved a palace.
But you understand secrecy.
You understand wanting something that did not belong to you.
You understand the strange insanity of risking everything for one moment.
You understand what it feels like when desire starts whispering louder than obedience.
You understand regret.
You understand consequences.
You understand wishing you could travel backward and stop yourself before one decision became ten more decisions.
David understood that feeling too.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from moral theater.
The Gospel does not say:
“Good people never make terrible choices.”
The Gospel says:
Sinners need a Redeemer.
But before we reach that Redeemer, there is one more royal woman we need to meet.
Her name was Abishag.
When David became old, his servants searched for a young woman to attend him and keep him warm. They found Abishag the Shunammite.
Scripture explicitly says David did not have sexual relations with her.
Then David died.
Solomon became king.
And Solomon’s older brother Adonijah—who had previously attempted to position himself for the throne—made what sounded like a modest request.
He wanted Abishag as his wife.
Bathsheba carried the request to Solomon.
And Solomon immediately saw something beneath it.
His response was essentially:
Why ask for Abishag?
You might as well ask for the kingdom.
That sentence is one of the clearest biblical windows into the political meaning surrounding women attached to a royal household.
Whatever Adonijah’s personal motives may have been, Solomon interpreted the request politically, in the context of Adonijah’s previous royal ambitions.
And that distinction matters.
We should not claim more than Scripture gives us.
The Bible does not contain a footnote saying, “Every relationship with every royal concubine automatically transferred legal kingship.”
History is usually messier than slogans.
But Scripture itself repeatedly connects access to women of the royal household with questions of succession, royal prerogative, rebellion, and claims upon the throne.
Rizpah.
David’s concubines.
Abishag.
Different circumstances.
The same disturbing political world.
Women could become symbols inside struggles between powerful men.
And suddenly an ancient story begins sounding painfully modern.
Because human beings still do this.
We still use people to acquire power.
We still turn relationships into leverage.
We still exploit sexuality.
We still confuse possession with love.
We still sacrifice people to ambition.
We still destroy homes because we wanted something.
We still call lust “freedom.”
We still call selfishness “finding myself.”
We still call compromise “complicated.”
We still hide behind language because plain words would force us to confront what we have become.
Kings had palaces.
We have phones.
Kings had harems.
We have secret conversations.
Kings had servants protecting their scandals.
We have passwords.
Different century.
Same human heart.
That is why the Bible remains uncomfortable.
It refuses to let us stare at David, Absalom, Adonijah, or Solomon long enough to avoid looking at ourselves.
The question eventually stops being:
“How could those kings do such things?”
And becomes:
“What would I become if every desire in my heart had a throne, unlimited opportunity, and nobody powerful enough to tell me no?”
That question is harder.
Because sin is easy to condemn when someone else is wearing it.
But Scripture is a mirror before it is a window.
Maybe your sin is sexual.
Maybe it is greed.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe you crave attention.
Maybe you manipulate people.
Maybe you secretly envy somebody.
Maybe you are addicted to approval.
Maybe you are carrying bitterness against someone who wounded you years ago.
Maybe everybody thinks you are spiritually strong because you learned how to smile while your soul slowly collapsed.
Maybe you know Christian language but your heart has wandered far from Christ.
Maybe you worship on Sunday and negotiate with temptation Monday night.
Maybe you are exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
One everyone knows.
And one God knows.
Be honest.
This may have started as an article about ancient concubines.
But somehow...
it found your room.
And now Jesus is standing at the door of the part of your life you hoped nobody would ever discover.
Not because He needs information.
He already knows.
He is standing there because you need redemption.
Not because typing a phrase saves you.
It does not.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops protecting the mask.
The ancient kings reveal something else too.
Power cannot cure the human heart.
David had a throne.
It could not cure lust.
Solomon had wisdom.
It could not guarantee faithfulness.
Absalom had beauty and popularity.
They could not cure rebellion.
Adonijah had royal blood.
It could not cure ambition.
And maybe you have been trying your own version.
“If I just earn more...”
“If people finally respect me...”
“If I find somebody who loves me...”
“If my ministry grows...”
“If my marriage improves...”
“If I become successful...”
“If I get enough followers...”
“If I can finally prove them wrong...”
Then I will be whole.
But there is no throne high enough to heal a sinful heart.
There is no bedroom intimate enough.
No applause loud enough.
No bank account large enough.
No relationship passionate enough.
No platform big enough.
No secret pleasure powerful enough.
Your deepest problem cannot be solved by finally getting everything your flesh wants.
You need something flesh cannot manufacture.
You need forgiveness.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need a new heart.
You need Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story of kings becomes breathtaking.
Because after centuries of flawed kings...
another King arrived.
But He was nothing like them.
Jesus did not accumulate women as trophies of royal power.
He treated women with dignity in a world that often reduced them.
He spoke with the Samaritan woman.
He defended the vulnerable.
Women followed Him as disciples.
Women stood near His cross.
Women became the first witnesses of His resurrection.
And unlike earthly kings who demonstrated power by taking...
Jesus demonstrated kingship by giving.
The kings of this world say:
“What can I take?”
Jesus says:
“I lay down My life.”
Earthly kings protected their thrones with blood.
Jesus left heavenly glory and shed His own blood for sinners.
Earthly kings used bodies to strengthen kingdoms.
Jesus gave His body to rescue people for His Kingdom.
Earthly rulers sacrificed others to preserve themselves.
Christ sacrificed Himself to save others.
Do you see the reversal?
The Gospel is not merely that Jesus is another king.
He is the King who exposes every counterfeit definition of power.
At Calvary, the One who possessed all authority allowed Himself to be stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Pierced.
Crucified.
The crown placed upon Him was made of thorns.
The throne men gave Him was a cross.
And above His bleeding head was the accusation:
KING OF THE JEWS.
They thought it was mockery.
He was accomplishing redemption.
The King was dying for rebels.
For adulterers.
For liars.
For hypocrites.
For sexually broken people.
For proud people.
For people carrying secret histories.
For people whose worst moments would destroy their reputation if anyone discovered them.
For people like David.
For people like you.
For people like me.
But grace does not call evil good.
Grace calls sinners out of darkness.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our chains with Christian vocabulary.
He died to redeem us.
Repentance means we stop defending the very thing from which Christ came to rescue us.
You cannot repent of the sin you insist on renaming.
Call lust lust.
Call adultery adultery.
Call pornography bondage.
Call greed greed.
Call manipulation manipulation.
Call pride pride.
Call bitterness bitterness.
Call unbelief unbelief.
Bring it into the light.
And then look at the cross.
Because the blood of Jesus is greater than the thing you finally found the courage to name.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal ignored.
Not scandal celebrated.
Not scandal rebranded.
Scandal confessed.
Scandal brought beneath the cross.
Scandal met by mercy.
A sinner forgiven.
A rebel reconciled.
A heart made new.
A story rewritten by Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years thinking your past disqualifies you.
David’s story should destroy that illusion without ever minimizing his sin.
David suffered consequences.
David was disciplined.
David’s family carried wounds.
Grace did not magically make every earthly consequence disappear.
But sin did not get the final word over the repentant man.
God’s mercy did.
That is why Christianity can look directly at scandal without surrendering to despair.
Our hope was never human perfection.
Our hope is Jesus.
Pray.
Even if the prayer comes out ugly.
Even if all you can say is:
“Jesus...I have sinned.”
Say it.
He already knows the chapter you are afraid to read aloud.
Bring it to Him.
Trust in Christ.
Turn from sin.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
Somebody reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars no longer belong to hopelessness.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be hiding.
Somebody may be losing a battle nobody knows they are fighting.
Somebody may have convinced themselves that God could never forgive what they did.
Somebody may know everything about church except what grace feels like.
And yes—even send it to the skeptic who thinks the Bible hides the failures of its heroes.
It does not.
Come back when temptation tries to convince you that secret sin has no public consequences.
Come back when shame tells you scandal is stronger than grace.
Come back when you need to remember the difference between the kings who took and the King who gave Himself.
Not as a replacement for your biblical responsibility to give faithfully and generously as God directs you, and not because anyone can purchase God’s favor.
Grace cannot be bought.
Your generosity does not make Jesus love you more.
But voluntary Christian generosity can help Gospel-centered work continue.
Sharing these articles publicly is another meaningful way to help the message travel.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you believe biblical truth should keep moving.
Do it as an act of willing generosity before God—not as a transaction with Him.
Then keep doing something even more important.
Love your church.
Help the poor.
Care for your family.
Give generously.
Serve quietly.
Forgive people.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
Open your Bible when nobody is applauding.
Pray when nobody is watching.
Obey Christ when obedience costs you.
Because Christianity was never supposed to produce spectators impressed by Christian content.
Jesus calls disciples.
And perhaps that is the final lesson hiding inside these disturbing stories of kings and concubines.
Human beings have always been tempted to turn people into possessions.
To turn sex into power.
To turn power into identity.
To turn desire into a throne.
To take.
To possess.
To conquer.
To hide.
But then Jesus entered our world.
The true King.
And instead of asking whose life He could take to preserve His throne...
He asked whose life He could save by laying down His own.
That is our King.
The King who knows your scandal.
The King who sees behind your mask.
The King who refuses to flatter your sin.
The King who calls you to repent.
The King whose wounds purchased forgiveness.
The King whose grave is empty.
The King who can take a story that should have ended in shame and write mercy across the final page.
So bring Him the chapter you keep hiding.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot control.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the wreckage.
Bring Him the crown you built for yourself.
Lay it down.
And follow Jesus.
And invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelievers—to follow too.
Because the goal is not merely to understand why ancient kings had concubines.
The goal is to recognize the King standing before us now.
A King unlike David.
Unlike Solomon.
Unlike Absalom.
Unlike every ruler who used another human being to prove his power.
Jesus Christ.
The King who did not exploit His Bride.
The King who died for her.
And when every earthly crown has turned to dust, every palace has fallen, every secret has been exposed, and every human throne stands empty...
the King who gave Himself for sinners will still be standing.
